title: Vaccinating sheep with Heptavac-P Plus
subtitle: The core clostridial and pasteurellosis vaccine for the UK sheep flock.
excerpt: Heptavac-P Plus is the most commonly used sheep vaccine in the UK, covering seven clostridial diseases plus pasteurellosis. Ewes vaccinated before lambing pass passive immunity to lambs through colostrum. Here is the correct vaccination schedule, injection technique, and what to watch for after dosing.
sourceNotes: Zoetis UK, Heptavac-P Plus summary of product characteristics (2023). NADIS, Clostridial Disease in Sheep. Moredun Research Institute, Vaccination in Sheep.

glossaryTerms.definition: A group of often rapidly fatal bacterial diseases in sheep caused by Clostridium species, including pulpy kidney (enterotoxaemia), lamb dysentery, struck, tetanus, braxy, and blackleg. Prevented by vaccination; treatment after onset is rarely effective.

Temporary immunity transferred from a vaccinated ewe to her lambs through colostrum in the first hours after birth. Lambs receive antibodies from the ewe rather than producing them themselves. Protection lasts 10–16 weeks.

content.text: and two strains of the bacteria that cause pasteurellosis. A booster given to ewes four to six weeks before lambing transfers
to lambs through colostrum. Lambs not given adequate colostrum in the first six hours will not be protected even from a well-vaccinated dam.
Naive animals (never vaccinated): primary course of two injections 4 to 6 weeks apart, followed by an annual booster. The first injection alone gives little protection.
Previously vaccinated ewes: one booster injection 4 to 6 weeks before the expected lambing date each year.
Lambs: vaccinate at 8 to 10 weeks of age with a two-injection primary course (4 to 6 weeks apart) if they are to be kept as flock replacements.
Warm the vaccine to room temperature before use. Cold vaccine is more likely to cause a lump at the injection site.
Shake the bottle gently to mix the adjuvant before drawing each dose.
Give the injection subcutaneously (under the skin, not into muscle) on the neck, behind the ear or in the loose skin of the armpit. Use a clean needle for each animal.
The dose is 2 ml per sheep regardless of weight.
Dispose of needles and empty vials as sharps waste.

A small, firm lump at the injection site is common and usually resolves within two weeks. Anaphylaxis is rare but possible. Observe sheep for 30 minutes after vaccination if possible, and have your vet's emergency number to hand during the dose event. Do not vaccinate visibly sick animals.
